paragraphs.text: Rammed earth is one of the oldest building methods in the world. Sections of the Great Wall of China were built with it, and in parts of North Africa and southern Europe houses made this way have stood for several hundred years. After a long period of neglect, the technique is attracting interest again from architects looking for low-carbon materials.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The basic material is a mixture of sand, gravel and clay, with just enough water to hold it together. The mixture is placed in layers about 15 centimetres deep inside a temporary wooden frame called formwork. Each layer is then pressed down, traditionally with a heavy wooden tool and today usually with a machine, until it is roughly half its original depth.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: When the wall reaches the top of the formwork, the frame is removed and moved up or along. The fresh wall can be left exposed at once, but it takes up to two years to dry completely. Many modern builders add a small amount of cement, usually between five and ten per cent, to make the wall stronger and more resistant to rain.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The walls are heavy and thick, typically 30 to 60 centimetres, and this gives them useful properties. They absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, which keeps indoor temperatures steady. They also regulate humidity, because the clay absorbs moisture from the air when it is damp and releases it when the air is dry.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: There are disadvantages. Building by hand is slow and needs a large team, and the method depends on suitable soil being available close to the site, since transporting heavy materials over long distances would cancel out much of the environmental benefit. In cold climates, the walls also need an extra layer of insulation.
paragraphs.label: E
